topicName: Secrets Management and External Secrets Operators
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Secrets Management and External Secrets Operators in Kubernetes"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Managing sensitive data like database credentials, API keys, and certificates securely is a critical part of running production workloads on Kubernetes. While native Kubernetes Secrets provide a basic mechanism for storing this data, they are stored in base64 encoding by default and lack advanced rotation, access auditing, and integration with external vaults. The External Secrets Operator (ESO) bridges this gap by securely syncing secrets from external secret management systems directly into your Kubernetes cluster."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Prerequisites and Architecture Overview"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"A running Kubernetes cluster (v1.22+ recommended)."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Helm v3 installed for deploying the operator."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Access to an external secret store (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault, or GCP Secret Manager)."},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"The External Secrets Operator introduces Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) such as SecretStore, ClusterSecretStore, and ExternalSecret. These abstractions define how the operator connects to the external API, fetches the data, and maps it to a native Kubernetes Secret."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 1: Installing the External Secrets Operator"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"The recommended method for installing the External Secrets Operator is via its official Helm chart. First, add the external-secrets repository to your Helm client and update your local registries."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"helm repo add external-secrets https://charts.external-secrets.io
helm repo update"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Next, create a dedicated namespace and install the operator using Helm, enabling the creation of Custom Resource Definitions during installation."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"kubectl create namespace external-secrets
helm install external-secrets external-secrets/external-secrets \
  --namespace external-secrets \
  --set installCRDs=true"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 2: Configuring a SecretStore"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"A SecretStore defines how ESO communicates with your external provider. In this example, we will configure a SecretStore targeting AWS Secrets Manager. Note that authentication can be handled via IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) or static credentials."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secretsmanager
  namespace: default
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: sa-external-secrets"},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 3: Creating an ExternalSecret Manifest"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"The ExternalSecret resource tells the operator what data to fetch from the SecretStore and how to structure the resulting Kubernetes Secret. The target section specifies the name of the Kubernetes Secret that will be automatically generated and updated."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: app-secret
  namespace: default
spec:
  refreshInterval: '1h'
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secretsmanager
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: app-secret-k8s
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
  - secretKey: DATABASE_PASSWORD
    remoteRef:
      key: production/database
      property: password"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 4: Verifying the Configuration"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once applied, the External Secrets Operator will query the external provider and create the target Kubernetes secret. You can verify the status of the ExternalSecret resource using kubectl."},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"kubectl get externalsecret app-secret
kubectl get secret app-secret-k8s"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"If configured correctly, the status of the ExternalSecret will report Ready, and the corresponding Kubernetes secret will contain the keys mapped from your external provider."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion and Best Practices"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"Using the External Secrets Operator allows organizations to maintain a single source of truth for sensitive data outside of Git repositories and Kubernetes etcd dumps. Always adhere to the principle of least privilege when configuring IAM roles or service accounts for the operator, and use appropriate refresh intervals to balance API rate limits with secret rotation requirements."}]
